###Amplitude in sinusoids of the form $y=a\cos(bx+c)+d$

The amplitude of a sinusoid of the form $y=\blueD{a}\cos(bx + c) + d$  is equal to $|\blueD{a}|$.  

 [[☃ explanation 2]]

options.explanation:
Recall that the graph of $y=\cos x$ has the following shape.

![A graph of a trigonometric wave on an x y coordinate plane. The x and y axes scale by one. The midline is at y equals zero. The highest points on the graph go up to one on the y axis at (zero, one) and the lowest points on the graph go to negative one on the y axis.](web+graphie:${☣ LOCALPATH}/images/b626efff0f07dc2b72aadd8c264e8b8841d0b941)

Here we see that the wave height is $2$, and so the amplitude of $y=\cos x$ is $1$. 

If $a>0$, the graph of $y=a\cos x$ is the graph of $y=\cos x$ stretched vertically by a factor of $a$.  If $a<0$, the graph of $y=a\cos x$ is the graph of $y=\cos x$ stretched vertically by a factor of $|a|$ *and* reflected across the $x$-axis.  A reflection of a sinusoid across the $x$-axis does not affect the wave height, therefore the amplitude of $y=a\cos x$ is $|a|$.  

In general, $y=a\cos(bx+c)+d$ is a transformation of the graph of $y=\cos x$.  However, the only transformation that will affect the vertical distance between the maximum and minimum values (and thus the amplitude) is a vertical stretch, which is determined by the variable $a$.  

So, the amplitude of $y=a\cos(bx+c)+d$ is the same as the amplitude of $y=a\cos x$, which is equal to $|a|$.
